1.title: Evaluating Accuracy: Hallucinations, Inconsistencies and Bias
1.text: Welcome to Module three: Evaluating Accuracy: Hallucinations, Inconsistencies and Bias. This module covers evaluating accuracy: hallucinations, inconsistencies and bias. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Why Claude can be confidently wrong, and what a hallucination is. The kinds of error to look for: invented facts, citations, numbers, outdated information, overstated abilities. How to spot inconsistencies and gaps (completeness). How bias shows up and how to reduce it. A practical evaluation checklist.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Confident Summary
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Confident Summary. A buyer asks Claude to summarize a new import regulation and gets a polished summary citing "Section fourteen(c)". The text reads perfectly, but Section fourteen(c) does not exist in that regulation. The buyer almost sends it to the compliance team.

1.title: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong
1.text: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong. Claude generates text that is likely and fluent. It is not a database of verified facts. The Help Center says plainly that Claude can produce incorrect or misleading responses, called hallucinating, a byproduct of current limits of frontier A I models.

1.title: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong, continued
1.text: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong, continued. The figure shows this: Why outputs go wrong: fluent text is not verified text, knowledge has a cutoff, context may be missing, and Claude may overstate what it can do. Fluent is not the same as true. Claude can write quotes that look authoritative but are not grounded in fact, and things that look correct but are very mistaken. Confidence is not evidence. A confident tone, or Claude rating its own confidence, is not a reliable accuracy signal.

1.title: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong, continued
1.text: Why Outputs Can Be Wrong, continued. Knowledge has a cutoff. Claude may not know events after its training cutoff and can get confused about current events. Web search can add current information, but then you check the cited sources. Missing context: if your prompt or files lack the facts, Claude may fill the gap with plausible guesses. Exam tip: Never use confidence or polish as proof. The right action for a factual claim bound for an important audience is to verify it against an authoritative source.

1.title: What to Look For
1.text: What to Look For. Fabricated specifics. What it looks like: Invented citations, section numbers, quotes, names, statistics, links. Example at Cedarbrook: A "study" no one can find; a U R L (uniform resource locator) that returns an error. Wrong numbers. What it looks like: Arithmetic or percentage mistakes, misread tables. Example at Cedarbrook: Returns rate eight percent when the table says six point four percent. Outdated facts. What it looks like: Information from before the knowledge cutoff. Example at Cedarbrook: A discontinued product shown as current. Overstated abilities. What it looks like: Claims to have sent an email, saved a file or checked a website when no tool exists. Example at Cedarbrook: "I've emailed the supplier" (it has not).

1.title: What to Look For, continued
1.text: What to Look For, continued. Misread source. What it looks like: Summary that distorts or omits what the document says. Example at Cedarbrook: A contract penalty left out. Over-generalizing. What it looks like: One case presented as the rule. Example at Cedarbrook: "Customers always prefer blue". Claude has access only to tools and connectors that are actually set up. It cannot send email or open an external site unless that integration is connected. If it says it did, check the destination yourself. Math: Claude can handle equations and calculations, but complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified with specialized software or by hand.

1.title: What to Look For, continued
1.text: What to Look For, continued. Links produced from memory may not work. Open them before sharing. Images: Claude does not create photos or illustrations the way an image generator does; it can build diagrams and charts, and it can read images you upload.

1.title: Completeness and Inconsistency
1.text: Completeness and Inconsistency. Accuracy asks "is it true?". Completeness asks "is anything missing?". Consistency asks "does it agree with itself?".

1.title: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued
1.text: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued. Completeness. Question to ask: Did it cover every part of the request and the source? How: Compare against your list of required points; ask "What did you leave out?". Internal consistency. Question to ask: Do numbers, names and dates match across sections? How: Scan totals and repeated figures; ask Claude to list all numbers it used. Consistency with the source. Question to ask: Does the summary match the document? How: Spot-check against the original; ask for the line it relied on. Consistency across runs. Question to ask: Does it give the same answer when asked again? How: Ask the same question differently; differences signal weak grounding.

1.title: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued
1.text: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued. Fit to purpose. Question to ask: Does it match the audience, tone and format you asked for? How: Compare with your prompt's constraints.

1.title: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued
1.text: Completeness and Inconsistency, continued. The figure shows this: Evaluate every output on accuracy, completeness and consistency, then on fit to purpose. Exam tip: An answer that is well written but incomplete or self-contradictory still fails evaluation. Check all three: accurate, complete, consistent.

1.title: Bias
1.text: Bias. Bias is a systematic tilt in output: unfair assumptions about groups, one-sided framing, missing viewpoints, or stereotypes. It can come from patterns in training data and from how the prompt is worded.

1.title: Bias, continued
1.text: Bias, continued. Stereotypes. Example: Job ads that assume a gender or age. What to do: Ask for neutral language; review against inclusive-language guidance. One-sided framing. Example: Competitor comparison that favors the first option named. What to do: Ask for balanced pros and cons; ask for opposing views. Leading prompts. Example: "Explain why our product is the best". What to do: Ask neutral questions; ask Claude to argue both sides. Missing perspectives. Example: Customer analysis that ignores a segment. What to do: Ask "Whose view is missing?". Skewed sample. Example: Conclusions drawn from a small or unrepresentative dataset. What to do: Check the data, not only the wording.

2.title: Bias, continued
2.text: Bias, continued. People decisions (hiring, performance, credit, benefits) need extra care: do not let Claude's output decide, and keep a qualified human in charge (Modules four and thirteen). Claude can help find bias: "Review this job ad for biased or exclusionary language", but you still decide. Bias is judged on the output and on the prompt. A leading question is a prompt-bias problem you can fix. Exam tip: When a scenario mentions H R, hiring, or customer groups, think bias review and human decision, not "trust the summary".

2.title: An Evaluation Checklist
2.text: An Evaluation Checklist. Re-read the request. Did the output do what you asked, in the format you asked? Mark every checkable claim: numbers, dates, names, citations, legal or medical statements. Test the risky ones against sources (Module four). Look for gaps and contradictions. Scan for bias: wording, framing, missing groups. Decide: ready, needs edits, or needs expert review.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Hallucination: Plausible but wrong output; fluent is not the same as true. Not evidence: Confidence, polish, Claude rating itself. Error types: Fabricated specifics, wrong numbers, outdated facts, overstated abilities, misread source, over-generalizing. Cutoff: Claude may not know recent events; web search plus checking sources. Abilities: Only integrated tools; check that emails and files really exist. Three checks: Accurate, complete, consistent (then fit to purpose). Bias: Stereotypes, one-sided framing, leading prompts, missing views; ask for balance. People decisions: Bias review plus a qualified human decides. Math: Verify complex or mission-critical calculations.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Claude's summary of a regulation cites "Section fourteen(c)" with great confidence. What should the associate do before sending it to compliance? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Confidence is not evidence; verify specific citations against the authoritative source.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which is a hallucination? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. An invented citation is a fabricated, plausible-looking detail.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Claude says "I have emailed your supplier," but no email connector is set up. What is true? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Claude only has tools that are actually integrated; verify yourself.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A report totals twelve in one table and fourteen in a later summary. Which kind of problem is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Numbers that disagree within the same output are an inconsistency to resolve against the source data.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An associate asks "Explain why our new tent is the best on the market." What is the main concern? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Leading prompts produce biased framing; ask for balanced strengths and weaknesses.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are reliable ways to check a Claude-generated statistic? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Independent sources and recalculation are the checks; confidence and detail are not.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Why can Claude be wrong about a recent event? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Training knowledge ends at a cutoff; use web search and check the cited sources for current information.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A summary reads well but skips a penalty clause that appears in the contract. Which problem is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. An omission is a completeness failure, even if everything stated is correct.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A hiring manager wants Claude to rank applicants and send rejections automatically. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. People decisions need bias awareness and human accountability.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. For a complex financial calculation that will go in a board paper, what is the best practice? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Complex or mission-critical calculations should be verified independently.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: C. Question three: A. Question four: A. Question five: B. Question six: C and E. Question seven: D. Question eight: B. Question nine: D. Question ten: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
